passage:
Thursday, 10:15 pm.

Payal messaged again. She says the extra banner set is "part of the deal," and if I don't do it by Saturday, she'll "have to leave an honest review" and the last payment "may be delayed."

I felt my stomach go tight. Reviews matter for my small design business, and I've bills. For about an hour I nearly said yes.

Then I calmed down. That's a pressure play, not a request. I checked the contract: banners aren't in it. I screenshotted every message and saved them in a folder.

I wrote back, kindly and firmly: "The extra banners aren't in the agreement, but I can quote them separately. The final payment is due under the agreed terms." I'm going to use the platform's dispute route if the payment doesn't arrive. I won't threaten her back.

Indu

qa.q: What did Payal threaten if the extra banners weren't done by Saturday?
qa.a: Payal said she would leave an honest review and the last payment might be delayed.

qa.q: What did Indu feel when reading the threat, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Indu felt the stomach tighten and nearly said yes, because reviews matter to the small business and there are bills to pay.

qa.q: What did Indu do that was wise?
qa.a: Indu checked the contract, saved every message, offered to quote the extra work separately and planned to use the formal dispute route instead of threatening back.

qa.q: How might Payal see Indu's reply?
qa.a: Payal may feel surprised that the pressure did not work, but the calm tone and separate quote leave a fair way to continue.

grounding: A client hints at a bad review or withheld payment unless Indu does extra; Indu recognises the leverage play, keeps evidence and stays courteous but firm.

"Trisha, the biryani was cold at my son's party. Unless you give me a full refund, I'll post one-star reviews everywhere. Every site."
"Zubin sir, I'm sorry you were unhappy. The food left my kitchen hot at seven. Your event started at nine-thirty, and the hall didn't have warmers, which I mentioned in my message on the 12th."
"I don't care about messages. Refund, or reviews."
Trisha's heart was pounding. She pulled up the chat on her phone. "I have the message, and photos of the food at pickup. I can offer a discount on your next order as a goodwill gesture. A full refund isn't fair to my staff."
"Then I'll ruin your name."
"If you post a review, that's your right. I'll reply politely with the facts. And if there's a payment dispute, I'll go through the consumer forum."
"You're threatening me?"
"No, sir. I'm telling you what I'll do. The discount offer stays open."

qa.q: What time did the food leave Trisha's kitchen?
What was Trisha feeling during Zubin's threats?
qa.a: She felt anxious and pressured, her heart pounding, but stayed steady and polite.

qa.q: How did Trisha handle the threat well?
qa.a: She kept evidence of the message and photos, offered a fair goodwill discount, refused a full refund, and named polite, formal ways to respond.

qa.q: How might Zubin see Trisha's refusal?
qa.a: Zubin seems angry and surprised, used to pressure working, and may feel cornered by her calm facts.

grounding: A client threatens bad reviews and withheld payment unless the protagonist gives in; she keeps evidence, stays courteous but firm, and uses formal channels.

passage:
I'm Vandana, and my first big home-staging client, Sabina, nearly broke me. Three days after I finished her flat for sale, she messaged: "I'll only release the final payment if you also style my sister's flat. Otherwise, my review will say you're unprofessional."
I read it on the bus and felt sick. My first instinct was to reply with something sharp, or threaten her back.
I didn't. Looking back, that was the best thing I did. I screenshotted every message: the original agreement, her approval photos, this one.
I replied, "Thank you for your message. The staging was completed and approved on 3 May, as per our agreement. The final payment is due. I'd be happy to quote separately for your sister's flat."
She didn't pay. So I filed a complaint through the consumer helpline, with the evidence attached. It took two months, but the money came. And the review never appeared.

qa.q: When was the staging completed and approved?
qa.a: On 3 May, as per the agreement.

qa.q: What was Vandana feeling when reading Sabina's message on the bus?
qa.a: Vandana felt sick and angry, tempted to reply sharply or threaten back.

qa.q: What steps helped Vandana deal with the threat?
qa.a: Keeping screenshots as evidence, replying courteously but firmly, offering a separate quote, and using the consumer helpline when payment was withheld.

qa.q: How might Sabina have seen Vandana's calm reply?
qa.a: Sabina probably expected Vandana to give in under pressure and may have felt thwarted by the firm, polite answer.

grounding: A client threatens a bad review and withholds payment unless extra work is done; the protagonist keeps evidence, stays courteous but firm and uses formal channels.
